feedback: Before this geometry races, the evidence is as follows. Iterations 2 and 3 used a 0.6 kg, 0.12 m body and gave oval progress of 0.44 and 0.45 with oscillation of 0.272 and 0.309. Iteration 1 used 0.8 kg, a 0.16 m body and a 0.12 m track, and gave oscillation of 0.173 but progress of 0.31. Yaw inertia (mass*(L^2+W^2)/12) is about 0.0027 in iteration 1 and about 0.0014 in iterations 2 and 3. So the evidence points to inertia, not track width, as the main driver of oscillation, although the two were confounded. Iteration 3 showed that widening to 0.10 m did not reduce oscillation, so I do not expect the track alone to help. The controller I wrote uses kp 2.8 and kd 0.35, between the iteration 1 and iteration 2/3 gains. Yaw gain rises as the track narrows, so I did not use the iteration 1 gain of 3.0 on this 0.10 m track. Max_error has stayed at 0.062 to 0.064 m on every track in every iteration, so it does not respond to these geometry or gain changes. Next race: if oscillation falls below about 0.2 with progress near 0.4, keep the inertia and move on to the reaction point. If oscillation is still high, the gain is the cause, not geometry, so stop chasing it with geometry. If progress drops below about 0.35 with the heavier robot, speed (wheel radius) is the next lever.
requested_changes: If oval steering_oscillation stays above 0.2 with mass 0.8 kg and body_length 0.16 m, keep the inertia and test wheel_track 0.11 m, because the narrower track has been raising yaw gain per command in every iteration so far.

If oval progress falls below about 0.35 with the heavier robot (iteration 1 at 0.8 kg gave 0.31; iterations 2 and 3 at 0.6 kg gave 0.44 and 0.45), try wheel_radius 0.035 m, since progress has tracked speed and the wheel radius is the speed lever.

If max_error stays at 0.062 m with line_loss_events at 0 and oscillation below 0.2 (every iteration so far has shown 0.062 to 0.064 m), move the sensor row to y = 0.02 m, because sensing has not limited tracking since iteration 1.
